etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English anticipacioun, from Latin anticipātiō, anticipātiōnem.

definitions.definition: The act of anticipating, taking up, placing, or considering something beforehand, or before the proper time in natural order.

quote.citation: c. 1599–1602 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Hamlet, Prince of Denmarke”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene ii]:
quote.text: So shall my anticipation prevent your discovery, and your secrecy to the king and queen moult no feather.

definitions.definition: The eagerness associated with waiting for something to occur.

quote.citation: November 20, 1836, Samuel Thodey, The Honour Attached to Eminent Piety and Usefulness
quote.text: anticipation of that final hour which he had long contemplated as near at hand

quote.citation: 1897 December (indicated as 1898), Winston Churchill, chapter VIII, in The Celebrity: An Episode, New York, N.Y.: The Macmillan Company; London: Macmillan & Co., Ltd., →OCLC:
quote.text: The humor of my proposition appealed more strongly to Miss Trevor than I had looked for, and from that time forward she became her old self again; […] . Now she had come to look upon the matter in its true proportions, and her anticipation of a possible chance of teaching him a lesson was a pleasure to behold.

definitions.definition: (finance) Prepayment of a debt, generally in order to pay less interest.
(music) A non-harmonic tone that is lower or higher than a note in the previous chord and a unison to a note in the next chord.

quote.citation: a. 1705, John Locke, “Of the Conduct of the Understanding”, in Posthumous Works of Mr. John Locke: […], London:  […]  A[wnsham] and J[ohn] Churchill, […], published 1706, →OCLC, § 25, page 81:
quote.text: [M]any Men give themſelves up to the firſt anticipations of their minds, and are very tenacious of the Opinions that firſt poſſeſs them; [...]
